title: Phage bet-hedging via 10,000-fold reversion, EBV humanized antibodies first appear
dek: Phages achieve bet-hedging through SSR's 10,000-fold reversion; EBV humanized antibodies block tumors in vivo; vaccines advance on multiple fronts.
why: From phage evolution to EBV antibodies to cognitive laziness, one thread connects molecular mechanisms, drug development, and science communication. The antibody data in the latter half is especially hardcore.
who: Researchers working on phages or antibodies, investors following EBV vaccine progress, and engineers who want to understand the plight of science communication.
skip: The first half hour of phage details is more basic; if you only care about antibody development, start at 50:44.

points.h: Phages deliberately let some progeny break
points.body: Jolene introduces a Nature Microbiology paper: homopolymeric nucleotide repeats (SSRs) in phage genes are prone to slippage during replication, causing insertions or deletions that shift the reading frame. This means a fraction of progeny always fail to make proteins properly. This randomness is the basis of bet-hedging: most sequences fit the current environment, but the persistent low-level variants may become survivors if the environment shifts dramatically. The population pays a small cost for long-term survival.

points.h: No need to pre-adapt: reversion is 10,000 times faster
points.body: The paper measured the reversion frequency of SSR regions and found it about 10,000 times higher than ordinary point mutations. This magnitude means phages can quickly turn a gene's function on or off within very few generations, rather than waiting for rare point mutations. Jolene emphasizes that this mechanism lets the population avoid pre-adaptation; instead, it relies on continuously generated diversity to be selected by the environment.

points.h: T7 has no SSRs, so betting is not standard
points.body: In the Basel phage collection, the T7 genome has no SSRs. Rich comments that T7 is 'businesslike'—straightforward, without these fancy mechanisms. This contrast shows that SSRs are not a standard feature of all phages but an evolutionary strategy in certain lineages within specific niches. Even among lytic phages infecting the same host, genome organization can differ drastically.

points.h: Humanization difficulty lies not in variable region but constant region
points.body: When converting mouse antibodies to humanized antibodies, there is a conflict between the variable and constant regions; someone must spend years adjusting the constant region to be compatible with the variable region to make a therapeutic antibody. Brienne says this was her 'aha' moment—she hadn't understood why mouse was necessary. Vincent adds that directly using human antibodies may not yield the desired antibody; the mouse platform's advantage is the ability to screen many clones and engineer the antigen, obtaining a full B-cell clonal diversification process, after which classic hybridoma technology is still needed to get monoclonal antibodies.

points.h: Hybridoma screening ends with only 10 antibodies
points.body: The group immunized mice with recombinant GP350 and GP42, made hybridomas, plated 384-well plates, and used antigen-coupled magnetic beads for high-throughput flow cytometry screening, testing binding and infection inhibition. Positive clones were subcloned and heavy/light chain genes sequenced, then expressed as recombinant human IgG1 antibodies. Ultimately they obtained 2 GP350-binding antibodies and 8 GP42-neutralizing antibodies. The whole pipeline shows the complete path from animal immunization to recombinant antibodies.

points.h: Antibodies also block EBV challenge in vivo
points.body: In two immunodeficient mouse models engrafted with human CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells, they injected 500 micrograms of antibody (ATX42-2, ATX350-2, MO1, etc.) intraperitoneally, then challenged intravenously with EBV and observed for 11 weeks. Results show these antibodies prevent tumor formation, suppress viral DNA replication, and block splenomegaly. Spleens from ATX42-2 and MO1-treated mice had no detectable EBER-positive cells. This means human antibodies protect against EBV challenge in vivo, not just neutralize in vitro.

points.h: Alum-adjuvanted subunit is dead; nanoparticle vaccines live
points.body: The GP350 subunit vaccine with alum adjuvant failed to induce protective immunity in trials; GP42 is conformationally variable, making it hard to elicit the right antibodies. But a GP350 ferritin nanoparticle vaccine has shown safety and immunogenicity in phase 1, with seropositive participants remaining EBV-free up to 540 days. Also in development are a GH/GP42 ferritin nanoparticle and Moderna's mRNA vaccine (containing four antigens). Vincent expresses disappointment that the paper did not test combinations of GP350 and GP42 antibodies.

points.h: Anti-vaxxers may lack not information but willingness to think
points.body: Vincent retweets 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' and quotes Joshua Reynolds: 'There is no expedient to which a man will not resort to avoid the real labor of thinking.' He argues that cognitive economy may partly explain anti-science and anti-vaccine attitudes: deep thinking is costly, and people prefer the effortless Type 1 thinking. He then says, 'That's laziness, cognitive laziness.' This view attributes the plight of science communication to humans' default cognitive mode rather than mere information deficit.
